newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall in nervous market ahead of Greenspan talk.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall in nervous market ahead of Greenspan talk.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Tuesday as investors succumbed to a last-minute bout of nerves ahead of the second phase of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Congressional testimony on the economy.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 66.20 points, or 0.96 percent, at 6,852.72, with nearly all the fall coming in the last hour of trading.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,357 to 1,107 on active volume of 536 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
But the Nasdaq Composite index ended up 6.19 points at 1,317.37 on the strength of technology stocks.
Evidence of the heightened tension appeared first in the bond market, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell nearly half a point, sending its yield up to 6.87 percent from 6.83 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"The stock market looked like it was just searching for direction," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities Inc. "It didn't have anything to make it go up and it had Greenspan to make it go down."

Greenspan, who on Wednesday will complete his semi-annual economic report to Congress, put financial markets in a state of high alert last week with blunt warnings on stock prices and interest rates during the first phase of his testimony.
Many Wall Street analysts viewed Greenspan's comments as an attempt to talk the market lower, and blue-chip stocks have declined with only a brief interruption since his appearance.
However, during an unrelated appearance on Tuesday before the House Budget Committee, the Fed chief denied his comments were aimed at affecting the market.
"That's not what I was intending to do," he told the House Budget Committee, later arguing he was incapable of affecting the fundamental course of the market.
"These are very thick, elaborate, international markets which are driven by decisions of millions of people," Greenspan said. "Nobody can affect them in a fundamental way."
Analysts remained unconvinced, however, noting that Greenspan's finger still appears poised on a key trigger, the one governing interest rates.

"There's still some concern about what he plans to do," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "He set the table last week for some preemptive action on interest rates."
Despite the broad sense of unease, several groups of stocks showed signs of life.
Technology and energy shares, which had been under heavy pressure in recent weeks, were among the session's strongest performers.

Texaco Inc. gained 3 to 101-3/4 to lead the Dow Jones index's gain. Shares in drilling companies also rose, among them Global Marine Inc., up 2-1/4 to 20 and Diamond Offshore Drilling Inc., up 5-3/4 to 61-1/8.

Among technology stocks, network companies attracted buyers after their extended sell-off. Ascend Communications Corp. rose 3-15/16 to 58, U.S. Robotics Inc. gained 2 to 57-3/8 and Cisco Systems Inc. rose 1-1/2 to 55-3/4.
Drug shares were broadly weaker, as investors took profits. Merck & Co. fell 2-3/4 to 91-1/4 and Pfizer Inc. slipped 2-1/2 to 90-1/8.
Among individual issues, Tupperware Inc. tumbled 8-1/4 to 35-7/8 after warning that its first quarter results would fall short of year-ago levels.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 4.36 to 790.95. The American Stock Exchange index rose 2.22 to 597.04.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.66 to 415.68. The average share was down 17 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,573.406 down 18.115 or 0.24 percent.
